# Rawley Z. Heimer

> Associate Professor of Finance at the W. P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University. Research on household finance, retail investing and brokerage, consumer credit, mortgage lending, consumer protection and financial regulation, and saving, retirement, and inheritance. Each paper below links to a page with the full abstract, a plain-language summary, a study-at-a-glance table (question, setting, data, method, main findings), and citation data.

Contact: rawley.heimer@asu.edu. Former Senior Advisor for Research and Policy at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and research economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland.

## Research topics

- [Retail investing and brokerage](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/retail-investing-brokerage.html): How retail investors trade, why they so often trade against their own interests, and how leverage, trading costs, brokerage practices, and social networks change their outcomes. Using natural experiments and account-level trading records, this research shows that limiting retail investors’ access to leverage cut traders’ losses without reducing market liquidity, that leverage constraints improve trading performance by curbing the disposition effect, that investors abandon their planned risk-taking strategies once gains or losses arrive, that social interaction spreads active trading and amplifies the disposition effect, and that higher brokerage commissions can raise rather than lower trading volume when brokers can steer their clients. The leverage studies use a U.S. cap on leverage in the retail foreign exchange market as a clean test of margin and leverage policy that applies to retail trading in stocks, options, and crypto assets.
- [Social media and finance](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/social-media-finance.html): How online social networks and social media shape what retail investors believe and how they trade. Using myForexBook, a social trading platform that linked members’ messages to their brokerage accounts, this research shows that joining an investor social network nearly doubles a trader’s disposition effect, that traders respond to peers’ gains but ignore peers’ losses so active strategies spread despite low success rates, and that the same platform data can be used to evaluate regulation such as leverage limits. The findings bear directly on research using data from Stocktwits, Reddit (WallStreetBets), X (Twitter), eToro, and other investor social media.
- [Consumer credit and debt](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/consumer-credit-debt.html): How households get, use, and repay credit, and how early-life conditions, cash windfalls, regulation, and politics shape credit access and credit outcomes. Studied mostly with individual-level credit bureau records, this research shows that households use cash windfalls mainly to pay down debt, that growing up on financially underdeveloped Native American reservations leaves people with lower credit scores as adults, that the Credit CARD Act’s age limits raised credit scores and homeownership by age 30 but increased mortgage delinquency, and that gerrymandering and senators’ political power reduce credit access.
- [Local banking and access to finance](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/local-banking-access-to-finance.html): How access to local banks and credit markets shapes the financial lives of households and small businesses over the long run. This research shows that people who grow up in places with less-developed local banking enter credit markets later and, as adults, have lower credit scores and more delinquent accounts, with effects that fade only slowly after they move away; that stronger local credit markets, driven by more predictable contract enforcement, raise small-business and household credit and incomes; and that banks cut lending to protected communities when they expect political relief from fair-lending enforcement. The studies exploit plausibly exogenous variation in local financial development, including differences created by federal law across Native American reservations.
- [Mortgage lending and housing](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/mortgage-lending-housing.html): Who gets mortgage credit and on what terms, how racial disparities in lending emerge, and how institutional investors affect local housing markets. This research shows how racial disparities in mortgage lending emerge: when month-end volume quotas push loan officers to approve more loans, the unexplained racial gap in approval rates shrinks by at least half, pointing to lender behavior. It also shows that expected political relief from fair-lending enforcement reduces lending in minority neighborhoods, that children whose parents had mortgage trouble in the 2008 crisis are less likely to buy homes, and that the growth of single-family REITs shows little evidence of harming local housing markets.
- [Consumer protection and financial regulation](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/consumer-protection-regulation.html): How regulation, supervision, and politics affect people who use financial services. This research evaluates limits on retail investors’ leverage, which reduced trader losses without harming market liquidity; the Credit CARD Act’s age restrictions on credit cards, which improved long-run credit outcomes at the cost of more mortgage delinquency; and consumer complaints to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where restitution depends more on who complains than on which firm is involved. It also documents how political power and gerrymandering weaken credit access and fair-lending enforcement.
- [Saving, retirement, and inheritance](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/saving-retirement-inheritance.html): How people accumulate, spend down, and pass on wealth over the life cycle. This research shows that subjective survival beliefs act like age-varying time discounting in the life-cycle model, helping explain under-saving by the young and slow asset drawdown by retirees, that expected inheritances raise consumption long before they arrive, that bequest motives follow a U-shape over life and rise sharply with wealth, that the wealthiest families move assets into private foundations at death rather than drawing them down, and that cash windfalls increase business formation but not self-employment.
- [Behavioral finance and beliefs](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/behavioral-finance-beliefs.html): Why people’s financial choices depart from what standard economic models predict. This research documents dynamic inconsistency in risky choice, with people abandoning their planned strategies after gains and losses; shows how social interaction amplifies the disposition effect and spreads active trading; shows that biased survival beliefs act like time discounting in life-cycle decisions and that people are overconfident about avoiding personal risks such as COVID-19; and examines how generative AI may change household financial decision making.
- [Legal and regulatory institutions](https://rawleyheimer.com/topics/legal-regulatory-institutions.html): How courts, regulators, and politics shape credit markets and what consumers get from them. This research shows that more predictable contract enforcement strengthens local credit markets and raises incomes, and that growing up with little access to local banks has lasting effects on credit outcomes, using the assignment of state rather than tribal courts on some Native American reservations as a source of variation in local financial development. It also shows that the prospect of political relief from regulators leads banks to cut lending to protected communities, and that CFPB monitoring of complaint handling raises restitution, especially for higher-income, more educated consumers.

## Published papers

- [Dynamic Inconsistency in Risky Choice: Evidence from the Lab and Field](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/dynamic-inconsistency-risky-choice.html): Rawley Z. Heimer, Zwetelina Iliewa, Alex Imas, and Martin Weber (2025). American Economic Review. Risk-taking is dynamically inconsistent: people plan to keep taking risk after gains and stop after losses, but instead cash out gains early and chase losses, in experiments and brokerage data.
- [Shale Shocked: Cash Windfalls and Household Debt Repayment](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/shale-shocked-cash-windfalls-household-debt.html): J. Anthony Cookson, Erik P. Gilje, and Rawley Z. Heimer (2022). Journal of Financial Economics. Households use cash windfalls mainly to pay down debt, timed to when cash arrives rather than to news of future income, which challenges forward-looking models of household debt; evidence from shale drilling payments.
- [Biased by Choice: How Financial Constraints Can Reduce Financial Mistakes](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/biased-by-choice-financial-constraints.html): Rawley Z. Heimer and Alex Imas (2022). Review of Financial Studies. Constraints can reduce financial mistakes: leverage limits improved traders’ performance by curbing the disposition effect, in retail trading data and in two experiments.
- [Personal Wealth, Self-Employment, and Business Ownership](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/personal-wealth-self-employment-business-ownership.html): Aymeric Bellon, J. Anthony Cookson, Erik P. Gilje, and Rawley Z. Heimer (2021). Review of Financial Studies. More personal wealth raises business formation but not transitions to self-employment, suggesting liquidity constraints matter differently for different kinds of entrepreneurs; evidence from shale mineral payments.
- [Politicizing Consumer Credit](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/politicizing-consumer-credit.html): Pat Akey, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Stefan Lewellen (2021). Journal of Financial Economics. Expected political interference weakens regulation: when a state’s senator becomes a powerful committee chair, credit to the state’s minority neighborhoods falls by 7.5%, driven by banks headquartered in the state.
- [YOLO: Mortality Beliefs and Household Finance Puzzles](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/yolo-mortality-beliefs-household-finance.html): Rawley Z. Heimer, Kristian Ove R. Myrseth, and Raphael S. Schoenle (2019). Journal of Finance. Subjective survival beliefs work like age-varying time discounting in the life-cycle model, helping explain why the young under-save and retirees draw down their assets slowly.
- [Should Retail Investors’ Leverage Be Limited?](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/should-retail-investors-leverage-be-limited.html): Rawley Z. Heimer and Alp Simsek (2019). Journal of Financial Economics. Limiting retail investors’ access to leverage cut high-leverage traders’ losses by 40% without reducing market liquidity, based on the 2010 U.S. leverage cap in the retail forex market.
- [Growing Up Without Finance](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/growing-up-without-finance.html): James R. Brown, J. Anthony Cookson, and Rawley Z. Heimer (2019). Journal of Financial Economics. People who grow up with less access to local banks enter credit markets later and, as adults, have lower credit scores and more delinquent accounts.
- [Law and Finance Matter: Lessons from Externally Imposed Courts](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/law-and-finance-matter-externally-imposed-courts.html): James R. Brown, J. Anthony Cookson, and Rawley Z. Heimer (2017). Review of Financial Studies. More predictable contract enforcement produces stronger local credit markets for small businesses and households, and higher incomes.
- [Peer Pressure: Social Interaction and the Disposition Effect](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/peer-pressure-social-interaction-disposition-effect.html): Rawley Z. Heimer (2016). Review of Financial Studies. Social interaction amplifies investors’ biases: joining an investor social network nearly doubles a trader’s disposition effect, the tendency to sell winners and hold losers.
- [Financial Decision Making, at the Dawn of AI](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/financial-decision-making-dawn-of-ai.html): Rawley Z. Heimer (forthcoming). Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Economics and Finance. Reviews why people’s saving, investing, and borrowing choices depart from what financial economics prescribes, and how generative AI might change them.
- [Subjective Beliefs, Saving, and Spending for Retirement](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/subjective-beliefs-saving-spending-retirement.html): Rawley Z. Heimer (2026). Chapter in Retirement Saving, Investment, and Spending: New Lessons from Behavioral Research. Reviews how beliefs about the future, especially about one’s own survival, change the predictions of standard models of retirement saving and spending.
- [Courting Economic Development](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/courting-economic-development.html): James R. Brown, J. Anthony Cookson, and Rawley Z. Heimer (2017). World Bank Economic Review. Uncertain court enforcement holds back long-run development: similar reservations under state courts grew faster than those under tribal courts.
- [Friends Do Let Friends Buy Stocks Actively](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/friends-do-let-friends-buy-stocks-actively.html): Rawley Z. Heimer (2014). Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization. Sociable people are more likely to invest actively than passively, consistent with word of mouth spreading active strategies; evidence from the Consumer Expenditure Survey.
- [Facebook Finance: How Social Interaction Propagates Active Investing](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/facebook-finance-social-interaction-active-investing.html): Rawley Z. Heimer and David Simon (2015). Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Working Paper 15-22. Investors broadcast their successes and stay quiet about losses, so social networks spread active trading despite its low success rates; evidence from a social trading platform.

## Working papers

- [Temporal Focal Points and Economic Outcomes: Evidence from U.S. Mortgage Lending](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/temporal-focal-points-mortgage-lending.html): Marco Giacoletti, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Edison Yu (2021). Working paper. Racial disparities in mortgage approvals emerge partly from lender behavior: when month-end quotas push loan officers to approve more loans, the unexplained 7-point Black approval gap shrinks by at least half.
- [Fallible Firms: The Economics of Consumer Redress](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/fallible-firms-consumer-redress.html): Charlotte Haendler and Rawley Z. Heimer (2025). Working paper. In CFPB complaint data, whether consumers get money back after complaining about a financial firm depends more on who complains than on which firm is involved.
- [Pushing Boundaries: Political Redistricting and Consumer Credit](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/pushing-boundaries-redistricting-consumer-credit.html): Pat Akey, Christine Dobridge, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Stefan Lewellen (2017). Working paper. Consumers lose access to credit when their congressional districts are gerrymandered.
- [Five Facts about Bequest Motives](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/five-facts-bequest-motives.html): Rawley Z. Heimer and Xiang Li (2025). Working paper. Bequest motives are stronger for people with heirs and the very wealthy, follow a U-shape over life, and people overestimate the bequests they will leave.
- [The Wealth Draw-down of the Fabulously Rich: Insights from Private Family Foundations](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/wealth-drawdown-private-family-foundations.html): Changhyun Ahn and Rawley Z. Heimer (2025). Draft available on request. When the eldest member of a very wealthy family dies, the family foundation roughly doubles in size, but charitable giving lags far behind.
- [Single-Family REITs and Local Housing Markets](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/single-family-reits-local-housing-markets.html): Marco Giacoletti, Rawley Z. Heimer, Wenli Li, and Edison Yu (2024). Working paper. Single-family REITs buy homes in neighborhoods ringing city centers, and their growth shows little evidence of harming local housing markets.
- [Brokerage Commissions and Trading Volume: Lessons from the 20th Century](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/brokerage-commissions-trading-volume.html): Valeria Fedyk and Rawley Z. Heimer (2026). Draft available on request. Higher trading costs can increase trading: under fixed NYSE commission schedules, higher commissions raised volume, consistent with brokers steering investors toward high-commission stocks.
- [Borrowing Young, Paying Later](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/borrowing-young-paying-later.html): Allison Cole, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Igor Livshits (2026). Draft available on request. Restricting young adults’ credit access protects them from early defaults but creates adverse selection later: after the Credit CARD Act, credit scores and homeownership rose by age 30 while mortgage delinquency increased.
- [Waiting for Wealth: Inheritances and Household Savings](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/waiting-for-wealth-inheritances-household-savings.html): Eirik Eylands Brandsaas, Rawley Z. Heimer, and Mateo Velásquez-Giraldo (2026). Draft available on request. Life-cycle models that omit inheritances overstate how patient households are; expected inheritances raise consumption and lower saving long before they arrive.

## Guides and policy writing

- [Navigating Credit Bureau Data: Field Notes for Researchers](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/navigating-credit-bureau-data.html): Rawley Z. Heimer (2024). Research guide. A practical guide to using credit bureau data in research: what it can measure, its limitations, how to acquire it, and how to merge it with other data.
- [Are People Overconfident about Avoiding COVID-19?](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/overconfidence-avoiding-covid-19.html): Rawley Z. Heimer, Haoyang Liu, and Xiaohan Zhang (2020). Liberty Street Economics, Federal Reserve Bank of New York. People expect their own exposure to COVID-19 to be well below what they expect for the general public.
- [Intergenerational Homeownership and Mortgage Distress](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/intergenerational-homeownership-mortgage-distress.html): Nicholas Fritsch and Rawley Z. Heimer (2020). Economic Commentary, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. Parents’ mortgage distress during the 2008 crisis is associated with a lower chance that their children buy a home.
- [Geographic Mobility and Consumer Financial Health: Evidence from Oil Production Boom Towns](https://rawleyheimer.com/papers/geographic-mobility-consumer-financial-health.html): Rawley Z. Heimer, Timothy Stehulak, and Caitlin Treanor (2016). Economic Commentary, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. Residents who move away from oil boom towns after the bust end up with stronger consumer financial health than those who stay.
